```{r}
#| include: false
require(mosaic)
require(gridExtra)
```

# Drawing from a normal population

We draw iid samples from a normal population,
but now look at the effect of using $s$ the sample
standard deviation, in place of $\sigma$.
Under this scenario, $\bar X_n$ has a normal
distribution for all samples sizes
$n$---specifically,
$$\bar X \sim \mbox{Norm}(\mu, \sigma/\sqrt n)
 \qquad\mbox{or}\qquad \frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n} \sim \mbox{Norm}(0,1).$$

We use simulation to look, instead, at a simulated
sampling distribution of
$$ \frac{\bar X-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}. $$
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| fig-height: 2.5
enn = 4
mu = 50
sigma = 6
runs = replicate(10000, {
 mySample = rnorm(enn, mu, sigma);
 xbar = mean(~mySample);
 s = sd(~mySample);   # compute sample sd
 (xbar - mu)/(s/sqrt(enn))   # I use s, not sigma
})
gf_dhistogram(~runs) |> gf_dist("norm") |>
  gf_dist("t", df=enn-1, color="red") + xlim(-5,5)
```
Note how the (red) $t$-distribution fits the
sampling distribution of $(\bar X-\mu)/
(s/\sqrt n)$ better than the normal curve does.

### Success in confidence intervals

When $\sigma$ was known, we chose $z^\ast$ for
a specific level of confidence and computed
endpoints of our interval as
$$ \bar x \pm z^\ast \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}. $$
Now, we propose simulating this to see how often
we are successful when $z^\ast$ is chosen from
the standard normal distribution, but $s$ is
used in place of $\sigma$.

```{r}
enn = 8    # sample size
mu = 50; sigma = 6; targetSuccessRate = 0.95
recordOfSuccess = replicate(10000, {
 mySample = rnorm(enn, mu, sigma);
 xbar = mean(~mySample);
 s = sd(~mySample);   # compute sample sd
 zstar = qnorm(mean(c(targetSuccessRate,1)));
 (mu > xbar - zstar * s/sqrt(enn)) & (mu < xbar + zstar * s/sqrt(enn))
})
manifestedSuccessRate = sum(recordOfSuccess)/10000
```
On this go, the rate of success, using critical
value 95% confidence level $z^\ast$ taken from
the standard normal distribution, is
`{r} manifestedSuccessRate`, a bit different from
the 95% rate advertised.

Let us repeat the simulation using $t^\ast$,
chosen from a $t$-distribution with $df=n-1$.
```{r}
enn = 8    # sample size
mu = 50; sigma = 6; targetSuccessRate = 0.95
recordOfSuccess = replicate(10000, {
 mySample = rnorm(enn, mu, sigma);
 xbar = mean(~mySample);
 s = sd(~mySample);   # compute sample sd
 tstar = qt(mean(c(targetSuccessRate,1)), df=enn-1);  # obtain critical value
 (mu > xbar - tstar * s/sqrt(enn)) & (mu < xbar + tstar * s/sqrt(enn))
})
manifestedSuccessRate = sum(recordOfSuccess)/10000
```
The success rate in 10000 runs using $t^\ast$,
not $z^\ast$,  is `{r} manifestedSuccessRate`,
more like the 95% rate advertised.

# Drawing from a non-normal population

If we change to a non-normal population, we
no longer have in place one of the tenets under
which the $T$-distributions were derived.  Still,
we might expect the coverage rate to be near
the advertised rate of 90% if we use a sample
size high enough to believe $\bar X$ has a
normal sampling distribution.
```{r}
enn = 8    # First we keep a small-ish sample size
alpha = 2; beta=8;
mu = alpha / (alpha + beta)
targetSuccessRate = 0.95
recordOfSuccess = replicate(10000, {
 mySample = rbeta(enn, shape1=alpha, shape2=beta)
 xbar = mean(~mySample);
 s = sd(~mySample);   # compute sample sd
 tstar = qt(mean(c(targetSuccessRate,1)), df=enn-1);  # obtain critical value
 (mu > xbar - tstar * s/sqrt(enn)) & (mu < xbar + tstar * s/sqrt(enn))
})
manifestedSuccessRate = sum(recordOfSuccess)/10000
```
The success rate in 10000 runs using $t^\ast$
on samples of size 8 drawn from a somewhat-skewed
beta distribution is `{r} manifestedSuccessRate`.

Next, we up the sample size to 30.
```{r}
enn = 30    # up our sample size
alpha = 2; beta=8;
mu = alpha / (alpha + beta)
targetSuccessRate = 0.95
recordOfSuccess = replicate(10000, {
 mySample = rbeta(enn, shape1=alpha, shape2=beta)
 xbar = mean(~mySample);
 s = sd(~mySample);   # compute sample sd
 tstar = qt(mean(c(targetSuccessRate,1)), df=enn-1);  # obtain critical value
 (mu > xbar - tstar * s/sqrt(enn)) & (mu < xbar + tstar * s/sqrt(enn))
})
manifestedSuccessRate = sum(recordOfSuccess)/10000
```
The success rate in 10000 runs using $t^\ast$
on samples of size 30 drawn from the same
beta distribution is `{r} manifestedSuccessRate`.
